meta.audience: All the people of Zarahemla, assembled at the temple
meta.location: The temple in the land of Zarahemla

world_behind.title: A quoted angel, and the king recedes
world_behind.text: Everything from verse 2 to verse 27 is a message Benjamin received and is relaying. He has spent a whole chapter reducing his own standing; here he steps out of the way entirely and lets a second voice carry the doctrine.

world_behind.title: The annunciation formula, a century early
world_behind.text: "Glad tidings of great joy" is the angel's phrase to the shepherds at Bethlehem. The same phrase, the same speaker type, and the same subject arrive here roughly a hundred and twenty years before the night in question.

world_behind.title: A name given in advance
world_behind.text: Verse 8 supplies "Jesus Christ" and names his mother Mary. This is the record's only pre-Christian naming of Mary, and it comes with a stack of titles piled on one person in a single sentence.

world_behind.title: Blood from every pore
world_behind.text: Verse 7 describes the suffering as producing blood from the pores. Luke reports sweat (Luke 22:44) "as it were great drops of blood." Where the gospel gives a comparison, the record states it flatly as what happened, and states it before the event.

world_behind.title: "The natural man" without Paul's vocabulary
world_behind.text: Verse 19 makes the same argument Romans 8:7 makes, that the unregenerate mind is at enmity with God, but the remedy offered is childlikeness. Submissive, meek, humble, patient, full of love: five qualities, all of them describable in a child.

world_behind.title: Little children, twice exempted
world_behind.text: Verse 16 says even if they could sin they could not be saved on their own, and the blood of Christ atones for them; verse 21 says none are blameless except little children. The record is taking a position on infant death inside an angel's speech, and Mormon will return to it in Moroni 8.

words.text: The angel's first word, and he says it twice. "Awake; and I awoke, and behold he stood before me" (v. 2), and then again in the next verse, where nobody is asleep any longer and the word has come to mean listen. Benjamin had asked his own people to awake to a remembrance one chapter earlier. The word he used on them is the word that was used on him, and the record puts it in that order.

cites.quote: Awake; and I awoke, and behold he stood before me

spans.text: Awake; and I awoke, and behold he stood before me

words.text: All-powerful. The King James Bible uses it once, at Revelation 19:6, of the Lord God reigning. The angel uses it four times in this chapter and Benjamin's people will use it twice more in Mosiah 5. It is this assembly's particular title for God: introduced by a messenger and adopted by a congregation.

Ordinary tiredness, and the word is not in the King James Bible anywhere. It sits in the middle of the angel's list of what Christ will endure: "temptations, and pain of body, hunger, thirst, and fatigue" (v. 7). Every other item there is an extremity, and the verse goes on to blood from the pores. Weariness is the plainest thing on the list, and putting it there keeps the suffering attached to a body that gets tired like anyone else's.

cites.quote: temptations, and pain of body, hunger, thirst, and fatigue

spans.text: temptations, and pain of body, hunger, thirst, and fatigue

words.text: A pattern that prefigures. It is the technical word for a person, object, or rite that stands for something later. Paired here with "shadows," and the pair occurs once in the record. It names what the law of Moses was doing, and the next clause says the people did not see it.

A testimony that gives off light. The angel says his words "shall stand as a bright testimony against this people" (v. 24), and brightness is not a usual property of evidence. In the King James Bible the adjective belongs to polished brass and to spots on skin that a priest has to inspect; elsewhere in this record it is what happens to swords that have been cleaned. Alma will pair it with a guilty man's recollection at the judgment, the nearest thing to an explanation the record offers.

cites.quote: shall stand as a bright testimony against this people

spans.text: shall stand as a bright testimony against this people

words.text: Formally handed over, the way goods or a prisoner are delivered into someone's keeping. What the evil are consigned to is not a place but "an awful view of their own guilt." The transfer is into a perception, and the misery follows from seeing rather than from being struck.

phrases.term: I am come to declare unto you the glad tidings of great joy
phrases.text: The Bethlehem phrase, spoken by an angel to a king in the Americas more than a century before the night it belongs to. Nothing is made of the coincidence. The angel says it as though it were simply the right way for a messenger to open.

phrases.term: Shall dwell in a tabernacle of clay
phrases.text: A body described as a tent made of earth. Tabernacle carries the whole Israelite association of a portable dwelling for God's presence; clay carries Genesis. Put together they say the incarnation in four words, and the phrase appears once more in the record, in Moroni's last letter.

phrases.term: Blood cometh from every pore, so great shall be his anguish
phrases.text: The anguish is given a cause in the same clause, the wickedness and abominations of his people, making the bleeding a response to sin. The verse has already listed temptation, pain, hunger, thirst, and fatigue and said this exceeds all of it.

phrases.term: His mother shall be called Mary
phrases.text: A name supplied before the person exists, in a list otherwise made of titles. The surrounding clause calls him Son of God, Father of heaven and earth, and Creator of all things; then, without transition, a woman's given name. The specificity is what makes the verse strange.

phrases.term: They shall consider him a man, and say that he hath a devil
phrases.text: The rejection is forecast in the terms the gospels actually use. Considering him a man is not an insult in itself; it is the whole error, and the angel puts it first, before the scourging and the crucifixion.

phrases.term: His blood atoneth for the sins of those who have... ignorantly sinned
phrases.text: A category defined by what a person did not know. Those who fell by Adam's transgression, who died without knowing God's will, who sinned ignorantly. All of them are covered without condition. The next verse draws the line, and the line is knowledge.

phrases.term: The law of Moses availeth nothing except it were through the atonement of his blood
phrases.text: The strongest statement in the record about what the law was for, and it is negative. Not that the law was wrong or superseded but that it never worked on its own. Signs, wonders, types, and shadows were all pointing, and the failure described is a failure to look where they pointed.

phrases.term: The natural man is an enemy to God
phrases.text: The charge is active opposition. Paul says the carnal mind is enmity against God (Rom. 8:7); the angel says the same of the natural man and dates it from the fall. What follows is a list of what replaces it, and every item on the list is a disposition rather than an act.

phrases.term: Unless he yields to the enticings of the Holy Spirit
phrases.text: An enticing is a persuasion, and the word almost always describes what leads someone astray; applying it to the Holy Spirit is a deliberate reversal. The Spirit does not compel; it entices. The verb belonging to the person is "yields." Neither term is forceful, and the whole transformation from enemy to saint is described as consent to persuasion.

phrases.term: Willing to submit to all things which the Lord seeth fit to inflict upon him
phrases.text: The hardest clause in the address, and it is placed last in the list of childlike qualities. Not endurance of what happens but willingness toward what is sent. The comparison offered is a child with a father, which is the only thing softening it.

phrases.term: They have drunk out of the cup of the wrath of God
phrases.text: Revelation's cup, and the reasoning attached is a comparison: justice could no more deny them this than it could deny that Adam should fall. The argument is that consequence is built into the arrangement from the start.

phrases.term: Mercy could have claim on them no more forever
phrases.text: Mercy given standing to make a claim, and then losing it. The whole passage runs on legal terms: justice denying, mercy claiming, a bright testimony standing at judgment. Alma will build an entire argument out of exactly this vocabulary.

verses.label: v. 2–3
verses.title: One word given twice with the obedience recorded between
verses.text: The record reports the summons, the response, and then the summons again: "he said unto me: Awake; and I awoke, and behold he stood before me. And he said unto me: Awake, and hear the words which I shall tell thee." The second use cannot be a repetition of the first, since the hearer is already awake, so the record has the same word do two different jobs in two verses. The whole of Mosiah 3 is delivered inside this frame, as a message quoted by a king who is quoting an angel.

verses.label: v. 5
verses.title: A list of miracles supplied a century in advance
verses.text: The record names six: healing the sick, raising the dead, causing the lame to walk, the blind to receive their sight, the deaf to hear, and curing all manner of diseases. Five of the six match the answer Jesus gives John's messengers at Matthew 11:5, which lists the blind, the lame, the lepers, the deaf, the dead, and the poor. The record's version substitutes a general clause for the lepers and the poor and keeps the rest in nearly the same order. Verse 6 adds a seventh item the Matthew list omits, casting out devils, and glosses it, "or the evil spirits which dwell in the hearts of the children of men."

verses.label: v. 7
verses.title: A physical detail stated as a measurement of anguish
verses.text: The record gives a bodily fact rather than a description of feeling: "blood cometh from every pore, so great shall be his anguish." Luke 22:44 has the sweat "as it were great drops of blood falling down to the ground," a simile; this verse drops the comparison and reports the blood itself. The clause before it sets a boundary, that the suffering exceeds what man can bear "except it be unto death," so the verse supplies both an upper limit and a physical sign.

verses.label: v. 8
verses.title: Two names given before either person exists
verses.text: The record names the son and the mother together: "he shall be called Jesus Christ, the Son of God," and "his mother shall be called Mary." Mary is named twice in the whole record, here and at Alma 7:10, and both are prophecies rather than narratives. The verse also stacks three further titles onto the first name, ending with Creator of all things from the beginning, so a naming prophecy carries a doctrinal claim about identity in the same sentence.

verses.label: v. 19
verses.title: An enemy named, and a remedy given as six qualities
verses.text: The record makes the diagnosis absolute in time, "the natural man is an enemy to God, and has been from the fall of Adam, and will be, forever and ever," and then attaches an escape clause. What follows is a list: submissive, meek, humble, patient, full of love, and "willing to submit to all things." Six terms, the last repeating the first, with the model stated twice as a child submitting to a father. The phrase "the natural man" occurs at 1 Corinthians 2:14 with a different sense, of one who cannot receive spiritual things.

verses.label: v. 25–27
verses.title: A drinking metaphor used three times in ten verses
verses.text: The record puts the same figure to work at verses 18, 25, and 26: "men drink damnation to their own souls," "they have drunk damnation to their own souls," and "they have drunk out of the cup of the wrath of God." Two of the three are identical in wording and the third supplies the vessel. Verse 26 then attaches a comparison that makes the outcome as fixed as a past event, that justice could no more deny it "than it could deny that Adam should fall because of his partaking of the forbidden fruit."

chapter.title: The king hands the sermon to someone else
chapter.text: Having spent a chapter insisting he is only a man, Benjamin delivers his doctrine as a quotation. The structure is the argument of Mosiah 2 continued by other means: the content does not depend on his office, and he arranges the text so nobody could think it did.

chapter.title: A life of Christ is given in the future tense
chapter.text: Eleven items run in sequence from verse 5 to verse 10 and none is out of order: the coming down, a tabernacle of clay, six named miracles, casting out devils, temptations and pain, blood from every pore, the name Jesus Christ, the mother Mary, the charge that he "hath a devil," the scourging and crucifixion, and rising "the third day." Two of them are proper names, which is the kind of detail a later text can be measured against; Matthew 11:5 supplies five of the six miracles and Luke 22:44 the blood.

chapter.title: Accountability is indexed to knowledge
chapter.text: Those who died not knowing are covered; the one who knows he rebels is not; the law was given because a people were stiffnecked; the knowledge will spread to every nation, and then none but children are blameless. The chapter's whole moral architecture runs on what a person had the chance to know.

chapter.title: The remedy for enmity is not effort
chapter.text: Verse 19 does not tell the natural man to try harder. It tells him to yield to enticing and become a child, and then lists six dispositions, none of which is a task. The strongest verb belonging to the person in the whole sentence is "yields."

chapter.title: The hardest clause is left unsoftened
chapter.text: Willing to submit to all things the Lord sees fit to inflict. The record does not explain, qualify, or promise that the inflicting will be light. The only relief offered is the analogy of a child with a father, and the reader is left to decide how much that carries.

chapter.title: Little children are the fixed point
chapter.text: They are blessed, they cannot sin to their own condemnation, the infant does not perish, and at the end only they are blameless. Every requirement laid on adults in this chapter is a description of returning to where children already are.

chapter.title: The chapter is built out of legal terms and ends inside them
chapter.text: Judged of righteousness, a righteous judgment, a bright testimony, judged according to works, justice denying, mercy's claim forfeited. Benjamin's own approaching trial framed Mosiah 2; the angel extends the same courtroom to everyone listening.

applications.title: Say where it came from
applications.text: Benjamin names his source before delivering his message. When you pass on something that matters, distinguish between what you were told and what you concluded.

applications.title: Locate yourself on the knowledge line
applications.text: The chapter sorts people by what they were in a position to learn. Ask honestly which side of that line you are on for the thing you are currently avoiding.

applications.title: Look where the pointers point
applications.text: Signs, types, and shadows were all doing their job; the failure was in the looking. Take a practice you keep faithfully and ask what it was meant to direct you toward.

applications.title: Let yourself be persuaded
applications.text: The verb for the person is "yields" and the verb for the Spirit is "entices." When you are stuck spiritually, the chapter's first suggestion is to resist less.

applications.title: Practice one childlike quality
applications.text: Submissive, meek, humble, patient, full of love, willing. Pick the one you are worst at and work on that one specifically for a week.

applications.title: Sit with the hard clause
applications.text: "Willing to submit to all things which the Lord seeth fit to inflict." Do not resolve it quickly. Ask what it would mean if you actually held it, and what you would need in order to.

questions.text: What do I think the anguish was for, and does my answer change how I treat my own sins?
Is there something I know I am rebelling against rather than something I have not understood?
Which of my religious habits have I started treating as the thing itself?
Where am I an enemy to God without having noticed?
Which of the six qualities is furthest from me right now?
What would it look like for me to be blameless in the way a child is, rather than in the way I usually mean it?
